title: Docker for a Node service
bridge: A Docker image is like your dist folder frozen together with the exact Node it needs. Except: it runs as a process on a shared machine, next to secrets. So we make it boring and hard to abuse. It gets a pinned base, no root user, and a filesystem it cannot write.
intro: The gateway, broker, orchestrator, Slack app and checks each ship as one Docker image, built like Byte's. This lesson writes that kind of Dockerfile for the notes service and runs it locked down. Then it shows the same rules in a Kubernetes pod.

picture.caption: Build in one stage, run in a small second stage, and start it with every lock on.

steps.text: both stages start from the same base, pinned by digest
stage 1: npm ci --ignore-scripts, tsc, drop dev dependencies
stage 2 copies only node_modules, shared and dist, and sets USER 10001
the service answers; writes to its own files fail

p: A Dockerfile is a list of steps. Each step makes a layer, and Docker reuses a layer when its inputs did not change. So we copy the package files first, install, and only then copy the source. A code change then skips the slow install.
This is a multi-stage build: the first stage has everything needed to build, and the second stage gets only what runs.
sections.because: We install from the lockfile before copying source because then editing a .ts file does not re-run npm ci.

code.text:
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:d6aa754f16b3197301076f047b5def2f02ea1dbbc2ca920407d46d7ec7f87b20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json .npmrc ./
COPY shared/package.json shared/
COPY svc/package.json svc/
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts
COPY tsconfig.base.json ./
COPY shared/src shared/src
COPY svc/tsconfig.json svc/
COPY svc/src svc/src
RUN npm run build -w svc && npm prune --omit=dev --ignore-scripts

notes.text: Node 24 on Debian bookworm, slim variant. The digest names the exact bytes, not a tag that can move.
Only the files npm ci needs. These change rarely, so this layer is usually cached.
The lockfile exactly, and no install scripts (lesson p1-1).
The source comes last: it changes most often.
tsc builds dist/, then dev dependencies (typescript, tsx, test tools) are removed.

p: The second stage starts again from the same base and copies only what the service needs: production node_modules, shared, and svc's dist. No compiler, no tests, no source of svc.
USER 10001 makes every later step, and the running process, use user ID 10001 instead of root. The ai-agents images and their pods all use 10001.
sections.because: We copy into a fresh stage because every tool left in an image is a tool an attacker can use.

code.text:
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:d6aa754f16b3197301076f047b5def2f02ea1dbbc2ca920407d46d7ec7f87b20
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/shared shared
COPY --from=build /app/svc/package.json svc/
COPY --from=build /app/svc/dist svc/dist
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "svc/dist/main.js"]

notes.text: Some libraries skip dev-only work when this is set.
Copy from the first stage, not from your laptop.
The workspace link in node_modules points here, so shared must come along.
A user and group with no name and no rights. Files in /app stay owned by root, so the process cannot change them.
Documents the port. It opens nothing; docker run -p does that.
The exec form: node runs as process 1 with no shell in between. The gateway uses CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"].

p: A tag like node:24-bookworm-slim moves: next week it points at a new image. A digest is a hash of the image's content, so it can never point at anything else. Byte pins its base by digest, and so do we.
docker pull prints the digest. A pinned digest only changes through a PR, and later Renovate opens those PRs for us (part G5).
sections.because: We pin by digest because a moving base image can change a build without any change in our repo.

code.text:
docker pull node:24-bookworm-slim
docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' node:24-bookworm-slim
docker image ls node:24-bookworm-slim --format '{{.Size}}'

notes.text: Prints the digest again, any time later, without pulling.
Fetches the image and prints its digest on the Digest line.
Prints only the size of the base, before our files are added.
Copy the digest you see into both FROM lines; yours may be newer than the one in this lesson.

p: Three docker run flags close the rest. --read-only mounts the image's filesystem read-only, so the process cannot write anywhere. --cap-drop ALL removes Linux capabilities, the small root powers a process may hold. --security-opt no-new-privileges stops any program inside from gaining more rights.
Byte starts its broker container with exactly these flags. The service needs none of what they take away.
sections.because: We start with every lock on because a service that holds keys should be able to do one thing: answer requests.

code.text:
docker build -t p1-lab-svc:dev .
docker run -d --name p1svc -p 8080:8080 --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges p1-lab-svc:dev
docker logs p1svc
CAP=$(docker logs p1svc | sed -n 's/^capability (shown once): //p')
curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $CAP" -X POST localhost:8080/v1/notes -d '{"text":"from docker"}'

notes.text: Builds both stages from the Dockerfile in this folder. The first build takes a minute or two.
No writes to the container's filesystem at all.
No capabilities: no raw network tricks, no changing file owners.
What the process printed: the capability and the port.
Same request as in p1-4, now against the container.

sections.ifInstead: If instead docker build fails at COPY .npmrc with 'not found', create the file: printf 'save-exact=true\n' > .npmrc. Also add a .dockerignore with node_modules, **/node_modules, **/dist, runs and .git.

p: Do not trust the flags; test them. docker exec runs a command inside the running container. id shows the user, and touch tries to write a file.
If a service really needs scratch space, mount a small in-memory folder with --tmpfs /tmp. Everything else stays read-only.
sections.because: We check the user and the filesystem from inside because one forgotten flag in a deploy would leave the service writable.

code.text:
docker exec p1svc id
docker exec p1svc touch /app/x
docker exec p1svc sh -c 'touch /tmp/x'

notes.text: The process user: 10001, with no name.
The app's own folder cannot be written.
Not even /tmp. Add --tmpfs /tmp to docker run if a service needs it.

sections.see:
uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001
touch: cannot touch '/app/x': Read-only file system
touch: cannot touch '/tmp/x': Read-only file system

p: docker stop sends SIGTERM to process 1 and waits 10 seconds. Node running as process 1 has no default handler for SIGTERM, so without ours it ignores the signal. Docker then kills it, and the exit code is 137.
Our main.ts closes the server on SIGTERM and exits 0 at once. Kubernetes stops pods the same way, so a deploy never cuts a request in the middle.
sections.because: We handle SIGTERM because every deploy and every scale-down stops pods this way.

code.text:
time docker stop p1svc
docker inspect p1svc --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'
docker rm p1svc

notes.text: SIGTERM first; SIGKILL after 10 seconds if the process is still alive.
0 means our handler ran. 137 means Docker had to kill it.
With the handler it takes a fraction of a second; without it, about 10.

sections.see:
p1svc

p1svc

sections.h: The same rules in a pod
p: On inf-rhinohealth these images run as Kubernetes pods (part p5). The pod spec repeats the same locks as settings, so they hold even if someone forgets a flag. G0-15's chart runs the gateway as user 10001 with a read-only root filesystem. G3-17 does the same for the other services.
sections.because: We write the locks into the pod spec too, because in the cluster nobody types docker run.

code.file: the container part of a pod spec (sketch; the chart is modules/ai-agents-service)
code.text:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true # same as --read-only
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false # same as no-new-privileges
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"] # same as --cap-drop ALL

notes.text: Kubernetes refuses to start the pod if the image would run as root.
The --read-only flag, written as a setting.
The no-new-privileges flag.
No Linux capabilities at all.

callout.text: Services that hold keys run as user 10001, read-only, with every capability dropped. The VM holds no keys at all; these images are where the keys live, so they get the tightest box.

quiz.q: Why is the base image pinned by digest and not only by the tag node:24-bookworm-slim?

options.text: A tag can move to a new image; a digest names the exact bytes, so builds only change through a PR
options.why: Byte pins by digest for the same reason, and Renovate bumps the digest in a reviewed PR.
The download is the same; the point is that the content cannot change under you.

options.text: A tag only works on Docker Hub, a digest works on ECR

quiz.q: The service runs with --read-only and tries to write a cache file to /app/cache. What happens?

options.text: The write works, because the app owns /app
options.why: The whole root filesystem is read-only, and /app is owned by root anyway.

options.text: Docker silently writes it to memory instead
options.why: Nothing is redirected; you get an error.

options.text: The write fails with a read-only file system error; change the code or mount a tmpfs for that path
options.why: Read-only is the default; scratch space is an explicit, small exception.

quiz.q: Which line makes the container run as a non-root user?

options.why: Every later step and the running process use that user and group.
It removes capabilities, but the process would still be root without USER.

words.plain: An image is the frozen files and settings; a container is one running process started from it.
A Dockerfile with a build stage and a smaller run stage that copies only what runs.
A hash of an image's content, like sha256:…; it never points at anything else.
The Dockerfile line that makes the process run as a user with no rights instead of root.
The container cannot write any of its files; set with --read-only or readOnlyRootFilesystem.
Small pieces of root power a Linux process may hold; we drop them all.
The process was killed with SIGKILL, usually because it ignored SIGTERM.

tickets.why: images.yml builds every service image: node:24-bookworm-slim by digest, npm ci --ignore-scripts, user 10001.
The gateway runs on inf as user 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, through modules/ai-agents-service.
The broker, orchestrator and Slack app pods run non-root, read-only, with all capabilities dropped.
The broker image is hardened like Byte's broker container: read-only, no capabilities, no-new-privileges.

remember: Pin the base by digest, build in one stage and run in another, USER 10001, read-only, no capabilities, and handle SIGTERM.
